text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
- Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen in parliament repeats Finland is not seeking NATO membership but will closely follow expansion's impact on the Baltic region and on NATO's and Russia's relations.
- Small companies are only now starting to invest in new capacity after long cautiousness due to poor profitability.
- U.S. president Bill Clinton's Helicopter surveilling Helsinki on Monday ahead of summit with Boris Yeltsin on Friday. @
- Poor cooperation between captain and pilot caused passenger ferry Tallink to hit a cliff outside Helsinki in April 1995, investigators say.
- Tampere-based Ata-Gears Oy has become leading Nordic and second European producer of cone-shaped cog wheels.

- Technology no hindrance to cooperation between Nordic bourses, although the Helsinki Stock Exchange has chosen an Australian system instead of the one planned for Stockholm, says Helsinki bourse managing director Juhani Erma. @

- Yrjo Niskanen, ex-head of the Pohjola insurance group, says he would not accept Pohjola's plans to devour mutual Suomi, which through cross-ownership is well-suited to remain Pohjola's de facto parent to prevent takeovers.

- Private work pension funds agreed on a model for interest rate on loans and industry spokesman Kari Puro hopes for approval from the ministry of social affairs and health, so plan to revive their loans to companies could go ahead from April. @
- Nokia Mobile Phones managing director Pekka Ala-Pietila says Nokia expects cellular phone penetration in Scandinavia to go over 50 percent in the year 2000. Five years ago, 25 percent was expected.
- Esa Harmala, chairman of the forest owners and farmers lobby MTK, says forest certification will be implemented in Finland if other countries adopt similar practices.
- City of Helsinki puts in extra efforts to gain image of a good host city during presidents Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton's summit. @

- New spheres of interest and grey zones in Europe would take it back to bygone days and the relationship between Russia and NATO must be arranged in a way that respects the security of all European countries, Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen says.
